runs.title: Young workers’ employment fell again in AI-exposed U.S. jobs. The cause is still open.
runs.summary: The September Stanford–ADP update extends the early-career employment warning but remains an exposure-based, nonrepresentative and noncausal payroll trend.

runs.title: Remote work challenges an AI-only junior-hiring claim
runs.summary: A four-country comparison weakens AI-exposure attribution for declining junior shares; newer French flows remain unresolved.

runs.title: French junior hiring fell faster in exposed work
runs.summary: French administrative flows and one AI-lab case sharpen the junior hiring warning; neither identifies AI-caused unemployment.

runs.title: Broad U.S. tracker still finds no clear AI jobs footprint
runs.summary: Yale’s October update reinforces a broad negative check without settling narrower hiring risks.

runs.title: AI-skill pay gap disappears within the same firm
runs.summary: A Swedish matched-hire study reports an AI-skill pay association explained by higher-paying firms, not a causal training return.

runs.title: AI narrowed a task-performance gap, not a job-offer gap
runs.summary: An Argentine randomized experiment tested task performance with AI access; no hiring or wage outcomes were measured.

runs.title: AI use reaches many jobs, but the survey did not count losses
runs.summary: A representative U.S. worker survey separates observed generative AI task use from job-loss claims.

runs.title: AI-written dissertations track career paths, not lost jobs
runs.summary: A specialized U.S. doctoral association raises a training question but does not change the measured jobs answer.

runs.title: Sector employment rose where AI could assist tasks, but use was unobserved
runs.summary: A U.S. sector study adds a bounded exposure-based counterpoint; the current hiring and displacement answer does not change.

runs.title: German AI-skill ads show no employment-growth link in the latest abstract
runs.summary: The 2026 journal abstract reports no total or skill-group employment-growth association in 2015–2023 German data; the current job-loss answer does not change.

runs.title: 6.1 million workers have low capacity to recover if AI displaces them
runs.summary: An occupation-level U.S. study adds a conditional vulnerability map, not a new count of layoffs or a personal forecast.

runs.title: Copilot studies split on hiring, but count different outcomes
runs.summary: A conference estimate of fewer technical hires and a journal association with more hiring months must not be averaged or turned into an individual forecast.

runs.title: A warning about student AI use lowered hiring ratings, not hires
runs.summary: A randomized U.S. survey finds employer-belief framing changes hypothetical graduate ratings, not observed jobs or pay.

runs.title: An AI-skills certificate improved interviews, not proven hires
runs.summary: A London field experiment finds more interview invitations with an AI-related credential for underrepresented women, but the effect is narrow and does not establish course value or job gains.

runs.title: Danish AI adopters slowed hiring, not layoffs
runs.summary: A Danish survey-register study links firm AI adoption to a narrow hiring slowdown, while self-selection and different study outcomes limit causal claims.

runs.title: Danish chatbot adopters did not show a sharper early-career drop
runs.summary: An author exposition of an already tracked Danish study adds a bounded employer-adoption comparison; U.S. and later cross-country findings remain unresolved.

runs.title: Factory AI-skill ads pay more, but workers’ wages were not measured
runs.summary: A Federal Reserve note separates broad AI-skill requests from rare explicit GenAI requests and unadjusted posted pay from worker outcomes.

runs.title: Job ads changed, but the study did not count layoffs
runs.summary: A U.S. posting study finds both role-mix and listed-task changes in an AI-exposure score; employer adoption and worker outcomes remain unmeasured.

runs.title: More startups did not mean more startup jobs in one U.S. study
runs.summary: A U.S. startup paper reports new entry offsetting incumbent job losses, leaving aggregate startup employment unchanged; a UK paper finds no clear entry increase.

runs.title: More startups in AI-exposed industries, not a jobs all-clear
runs.summary: A CEPR abstract adds an entry-linked labor counter-signal while leaving causal effects and incumbent outcomes unresolved.

runs.title: AI exposure scores predicted only a small part of firm use.
runs.summary: A Census measurement study limits the leap from exposed work to employer AI adoption, without erasing narrow hiring warnings.

runs.title: Junior software ads fell relative to senior ads. The AI share is unknown.
runs.summary: A newly reviewed U.S. posting study adds a specific entry-route warning while leaving completed hires and AI attribution unresolved.

runs.title: An AI job-risk score changed with the platform supplying its data.
runs.summary: A methodological preprint shows that platform user selection can change employment estimates built from platform-derived exposure, without measuring a new job loss.

runs.title: AI-written pitches made experience harder to judge in a controlled test. They did not show fewer hires.
runs.summary: An experimental screening result narrows a previously theoretical concern but cannot establish real hiring or employment effects.

runs.title: Posted pay rose. Relative pay for workers who stayed fell in AI-exposed U.S. occupations.
runs.summary: A Cleveland Fed occupation-level comparison adds a realized-pay and churn signal, but cannot isolate AI causation.

runs.title: AI interviews raised offers in one experiment. That does not mean more jobs.
runs.summary: A randomized Philippine customer-service hiring experiment found 12% more offers after AI voice interviews than human interviews; the result is bounded to one hiring stage and firm.

runs.title: AI may change hiring before the interview. A new theory explains how.
runs.summary: A new formal model identifies a possible entry barrier when AI makes applications less informative and employers lean more on prior experience. It is a mechanism, not evidence of real hiring effects.

runs.title: AI-exposed jobs posted higher pay. Their entry-level share still collapsed.
runs.summary: A new U.S. job-posting analysis finds faster advertised-pay growth in highly AI-exposed occupations but a sharp shift from entry-level to senior ads, complicating both wage-collapse and all-clear claims.

runs.title: Texas graduate records deepen the early-career AI warning. They do not prove the cause.
runs.summary: A new Texas administrative-record study links higher major-level GenAI exposure to lower first-year employment and earnings, adding an independent regional signal beside the broad U.S. null and the graduate-unemployment counter-signal.

runs.title: AI adopters shifted toward senior workers. That is not a layoff wave.
runs.summary: A new 41-country adoption study finds a lower junior share and higher senior employment at AI-adopting multinational affiliates, adding a bounded reorganization signal beside the broad U.S. null.

runs.title: The broad U.S. AI jobs check still cannot find a clear footprint.
runs.summary: Yale’s update with August CPS data limits an economy-wide AI layoff claim while leaving narrower entry-level and regional warnings unresolved.

runs.title: Swedish AI grants raised vacancy posting without a detected headcount effect
runs.summary: A Swedish grant study separates more job ads from completed hiring and total employment.

runs.title: A 4% AI jobs figure is a scenario. It is not evidence that 4% of jobs are gone.
runs.summary: A new CEPR model illustrates a 2030 cognitive-employment decline under one conditional path; it changes the forecast boundary, not the measured evidence of current job loss.

runs.title: AI adopters hired less in Denmark. That is a warning, not an economy-wide layoff verdict.
runs.summary: A new Danish firm-record study links reported AI adoption to lower recruitment and slower employment growth at smaller firms, while California claims data limit any broad unemployment claim.

runs.title: The national graduate AI unemployment alarm just met a hard counter-signal.
runs.summary: A new U.S. CPS study finds no statistically significant summer unemployment spike among recent college graduates, narrowing but not erasing the entry-level warning.

runs.title: Texas just broke the “no AI hiring signal” story. It did not prove layoffs.
runs.summary: A Texas posting analysis adds a regional AI-exposure warning, while broad U.S. posting results still limit any national conclusion.

runs.title: The early-career AI warning just hit a hard Nordic counter-signal.
runs.summary: Population-wide Norwegian records find no robust young-worker employment displacement, sharpening the country and attribution limits on U.S. exposure-based warnings.

runs.title: The first AI-spending jobs test points up. The entry-level verdict is still open.
runs.summary: A firm-level spending proxy adds an actual-adoption counterpoint to the exposure-based early-career warning without resolving causal attribution.

runs.title: The 19% early-career gap got bigger. The causal fight did too.
runs.summary: A revised payroll study reinforces the concentrated U.S. early-career warning, while a cross-country remote-work result makes the attribution question sharper.

runs.title: A second Census study raises the stakes for AI-exposed graduates. It still is not a final verdict.
runs.summary: A new Census graduate study strengthens the concentrated U.S. early-career warning, while broad job-posting research finds no distinct AI-driven decline.

runs.title: The first hard warning is early-career hiring. It is not yet a clean AI verdict.
runs.summary: A U.S. working paper finds a sharp relative decline in early-career hiring in high-AI-exposure industries, while its AI attribution remains unresolved.
